title: The Arctic's melting ice caps uncover the world's next battleground
subtitle: The real reason Trump wanted Greenland
author: Rana Foroohar
introduction: The battle over the Arctic shows why China’s economic philosophy is superior to America’s, argues Financial Times columnist Rana Foroohar in an interview with IAI’s Felix Butcher. As melting ice opens shipping routes in the Arctic and access to resources, power belongs to those with the industrial might to seize it. America assumed markets knew best and let its industry decline. China saw industrial and military power as connected. It prioritised shipbuilding, and now has 5,500 ocean-going vessels compared to fewer than 200 for America. America’s free-market fundamentalism showed a flawed understanding of geopolitical power. Building things matters.
body:
Felix Butcher: You’re a Financial Times columnist and the author of several books, including most recently Sea Change: America’s New Great Game in the Arctic Circle. You argue that the Arctic is becoming the next arena for great power competition between the US, China and Russia. Could you explain why that is?

Rana Foroohar: In a couple of words: global warming. Nobody cared as much about what was happening in the Arctic until the poles started to melt. Arctic climate change is proceeding at a more rapid rate than climate change in other parts of the world, and one of the results of this is that the ice that had covered large swaths of the Arctic is now melting. The result of that is that transportation pathways are opening up. So you can now get ships through several months out of the year.

In fact, in September, China launched the first weekly shipping route across the poles, through the Northern Sea Route, which is largely controlled by Russia. This is a way of getting around choke points in the Strait of Hormuz, Suez Canal, Panama Canal, etc.

At the same time, you’ve got the US suddenly taking an interest in places like Greenland, and you’ve got a US-Canada trade war. There’s a race for rare earth minerals and for natural gas. Fishing in the Arctic is very rich still; it’s one of the largest untapped sources of protein on the planet. So there’s a lot going on in the Arctic.

In this book, not only did I take a trip up on America’s only icebreaker in the high north, which is the kind of ship that’s required to get up to the Arctic, but I also looked at the way in which the paradigm today really mirrors the great game of the nineteenth century. That was the rivalry between the British Empire and the Russian Empire that went on for decades, a hundred years by some measures. It roped in buffer states; you had countries coming in and out of the conflict at different times and in different theaters. That’s very much the paradigm that we’re headed for today, and the Arctic is a perfect example of it.

We’ve often heard the US-China conflict referred to in terms of a kind of Athens-Sparta, a one-and-done conflict: “The US is going to win, China is going to win.” But I’m saying: actually, it’s much more complicated. Just as in the nineteenth century, there are three aspects to this competitive rivalry: mapping, mining, and mercantilism. And these things are really happening in force in the Arctic. If you look back at the nineteenth century, there was a race where the Russians wanted to be able to get a passage to India to capture some of the wealth that the British had enjoyed there. You had a lot of mapping of the Central Asian republics, of these pathways, in order to get to India. And the driving force behind all of it was mercantilism, the riches that fuelled empire.

If you look at what’s happening in the Arctic today, there is a huge effort currently underway to map the ocean floor. And why does that matter? You would think that with satellite technology we could see what’s going on. In order to chart a safe passage for sea travel for transport, but also to really understand where mineral and natural gas resources might be, you need sonar mapping, which means sending ships to the area.

The entire chessboard has just been thrown up and the Arctic is a perfect place to look at how the pieces might be landing.

And one of the things that I did when I was on, at that time the only US Coast Guard icebreaker in the Arctic, the Healy, was work with scientists mapping the ocean seabed. And we discovered things like a methane-plumed volcano that could have been a new natural gas discovery (there are public and private entities looking into that right now). We were trying to discover a navigable path through the Northwest Passage, which is one of the passages most likely to be used by Western powers that are looking to do more commercial transport in the area.

When you look at the world from the top down, which is how all of the maps on board the ships look at the world, you have an entirely different picture of what’s happening. For starters, Russia is over half of the landmass in the area. Russia is very close to the US (Alaska used to be part of Russian territory, of course). You also see that Canada is much more important, and Greenland is important. But the US is kind of small. And also certain Asian countries, Japan, South Korea, China (which has declared itself a near-Arctic nation), are much closer than you might imagine. Again, there are these huge comparisons to be made with the nineteenth-century Great Game.

I think that this US-China spheres of influence competition is going to go on for decades. You’re going to see many countries, for example Canada and European nations, sometimes siding with the US, but possibly sometimes siding with China. You saw Mark Carney, after Trump launched a trade war, saying Canada is going to do more trade with China, and is going to loop in European allies into a new alliance of middle powers. It’s as though the entire chessboard has just been thrown up and the Arctic is a perfect place to look at how the pieces might be landing.

Could you explain what geoeconomics is and why it’s particularly relevant in the far north?

In the US and the Anglo-American world in general, since the Reagan-Thatcher Revolution we’ve had an idea that the markets always know best. But I think really since the financial crisis, certainly since COVID, the war in Ukraine, US-China trade wars, and more tension in the South China Sea, we’re all realizing that state power matters, place matters, making things matters again, which is often something that is pushed by the state.

If you look at how China, for example, has ring-fenced maritime and sea power, that’s because the state decided in the early 2000s that this should be an important sector, and that China would come to own this sector, and they poured all kinds of state resources into doing that.

Russia is sort of a vassal nation to China. It’s got the resources, but China has the strategy.

Now China has stakes in over half of the major ports in the world. It has 5,500 ocean-going vessels. That’s compared to under 200 for the US. This is the bricks and mortar of globalization, because 80% of trade goes by ship. And most military vessels are supported by commercial ships, most of which are made in China. All of that is driven by the state.

The US said: “Let the markets do what they’re going to do.” There was a lot of outsourcing, not just of shipbuilding, but of chip building, complex machinery, automobiles, PPE, biopharmaceuticals, et cetera. And now there’s a pendulum shift back to this idea that we need resiliency at home. We need to be able to, if not in-country, at least regionally or with allies, make more of what we might need in a pinch.

There is a new alliance to build icebreakers. The US and Finland are going to be doing that. Eventually that may loop in Canada, South Korea, Japan, Italy even. It’s a nascent look into what a post-neoliberal security and trade paradigm might look like.

What is the relationship between a country’s industrial capacity and its military strength, and do you think that relationship has been underestimated by the West?

In historical terms, there wasn’t a separation between commercial entities and the state. You could have private companies, but they were always in some ways in service to state power. If a factory could produce munitions, it might also be able to produce buggies or who-knows-what. There was that interlinkage.

Asian countries, particularly China, picked up on that. They structured their economy in such a way that commercial and military were always together. That’s the nature of state capitalism in general and the way the Communist Party works. You create economies of scale that way. You create efficiency.

I’ll give you an example. There was a factory I visited once in Chongqing in Western China that had been making munitions up until the Cold War. The minute that there’s glasnost, the Berlin Wall falls, and they start making bicycles. And then, later on, they go higher up the food chain, and they’re making cars. And now they might be making dual-use military-civilian equipment. It’s in this sense that you don’t disconnect those two things.

In the US, there was something a couple of decades ago called the peace dividend, which was the idea that we don’t need to make things anymore, particularly we don’t need to have military might, because we’ve reached the end of history. Communism is over, all boats are rising, the world is flat. We know now that’s not the case. So there is this rush, both in North America and also in Europe, to reindustrialize, to figure out how we can have the capacity to protect our own security and make sure our citizens have things that they need if there is a pandemic or a war.

The icebreaker deal is a good window into that. I got interested in this deal, which was announced in 2024, because it seemed like a little gem of friendshoring. Friendshoring is the idea that the US can’t go it alone. No country can go it alone.

The Chinese and Russians together have between 45 and 60 operational icebreakers. That’s quite a lot of power relative to the US.

Trump was the first president to say “let’s build icebreakers with the Finns,” at the very end of Trump 1. Biden comes in, and his team does what Democrats do, which is think and put meat on the bones of this idea and create a real policy around it. Unfortunately, like Democrats, they also want to bring consensus through all the interest groups. And so there was a lot of “What part of this should go to allies, what part should go to domestic labor?” Trump 2 comes in, and he does what Republicans do, which is just sign things and get stuff going. And he stopped worrying so much about domestic workers and just said to the Finns: you build the first four icebreakers, we’ll figure out how to do it later.

And we’re now off to the races. That shows you how it takes not just one, but sometimes two or three administrations to turn the needle on something like the conventional trade and industrial paradigm.

In the book, you reference Alfred Thayer Mahan’s arguments that in order to be a great power, you need to have a powerful maritime industry. Today, the US is significantly behind China in that respect. What’s the significance of that for the future of world politics?

Shortly after coming into the WTO in 2001, China decided to make the maritime sector a state-controlled sector. They put all the effort behind it. They developed the One Belt, One Road strategy (now the Belt and Road Initiative), which was about essentially ring-fencing commerce and supply chains through the old Silk Road. In 2016, they added a line about a polar Silk Road. We think about Russia as being the big Arctic power. I think Russia is sort of a vassal nation to China. It’s got the resources, but China has the strategy. And so you see this connection all throughout Eurasia and now up into the Arctic, of Chinese logistical power.

America at this point builds around 0.1-0.2% of all the world’s ships by tonnage. China has most of the capacity. If it wanted to create a blockade or take back some of its own ships at a time of crisis, in the way that it briefly took back some of its own PPE during COVID, it would be able to do so very easily. A lot of people think, going back to Mahan, that America still has the world’s biggest and best Navy. That may be true, but think about the fact that 80 or 90% of all supplies during wartime are provided by commercial vessels. America does not have that capacity. In two decades, with long-term planning, China has been able to dominate the bricks and mortar of globalization, which is maritime. America has completely given that up.
